# Cell-to-Landline Gateway for Gate Systems

This is a really common problem, and there are actual commercial products designed exactly for this. You don't need to hack anything together.

## Dedicated Products

**Cellular Fixed Wireless Terminals (FWT)** - these are the standard solution:

- **XLink BT** (Xtreme Technologies BTTN) - Bluetooth pairs with your cell phone, provides a standard RJ-11 jack with dial tone. ~$50-60
- **Phonetone / Telular / Premicell GSM Fixed Wireless Terminals** - takes a SIM card, provides RJ-11 output with dial tone
- **YX300-GSM** or similar GSM gateways on Amazon - budget option, same concept

## How It Works

```
Gate system calls your "unit number"
        ↓
Signal goes to your wall jack (RJ-11)
        ↓
FWT/Gateway picks up the line
        ↓
Routes to your cell phone (via Bluetooth or SIM)
        ↓
You press "9" (or whatever) to buzz them in
```

## Setup

1. Plug the gateway into your existing RJ-11 wall jack
2. Pair it with your cell phone (Bluetooth models) or insert a cheap SIM/prepaid card (cellular models)
3. When the gate system sends the ring signal, the gateway converts it and rings your cell
4. You answer and press the DTMF tone to open the gate

## The XLink BT Specifically

This is the most popular for exactly your scenario:
- Pairs via Bluetooth to your smartphone
- Generates a real dial tone on the RJ-11 jack
- The gate intercom thinks it's talking to a landline
- You answer on your cell from anywhere in range (~30 ft for BT, or get the cellular SIM version for unlimited range)

## If You Need More Range

Get a **GSM fixed wireless terminal** with its own SIM card instead of Bluetooth. Then it works even when you're not home. A cheap prepaid data/voice SIM costs a few dollars a month.

Search Amazon for **"fixed wireless terminal RJ11"** or **"cellular to landline adapter"** and you'll find dozens of options from $30-80.

This is a super common problem with old gate/intercom systems (usually called "telephone entry systems" like DoorKing, Linear, Chamberlain, Viking, etc.). You don't need to hack or fake anything — there are off-the-shelf products designed for exactly your situation. They're called **cellular terminals**, **VoIP ATAs**, or **GSM/4G FXS gateways**.

Here are the main approaches, cheapest to most reliable:

## Option 1: Cellular Terminal (best for gates)
These are purpose-built boxes with a SIM card that present an RJ11 jack looking like a real landline (dial tone, ring voltage, DTMF). You wire the two wires from your wall jack into the device instead of the (dead) phone line.

Look for:
- **Yeastar TG100** (single SIM, 4G)
- **Dinstar UC2000** series
- **Portech MV-372**
- Various "4G FCT" or "4G Fixed Wireless Terminal" units on Amazon (Etross, Huawei, etc.) — $60–$200

You'll need a cheap voice-capable SIM (Tello, Red Pocket, US Mobile, or a prepaid AT&T/T-Mobile plan — note Verizon is picky about third-party devices). Pop it in, plug the two wires from your gate into the FXS port, done.

## Option 2: VoIP ATA + softphone/number
If you have decent Wi-Fi near the gate controller (it's usually in your unit, not outside), this is cheaper and more reliable than cellular:

- **Grandstream HT801** (~$35) or **Cisco SPA112** (~$50)
- Pair with a VoIP provider: VOIP.ms ($1–3/month), Google Voice (free, via a bridge like Obi), or Anveo.

The ATA plugs into Ethernet, provides dial tone on an RJ11 jack, and your gate system sees it as a landline.

## Wiring
Dead simple — gate entry systems use two wires (tip and ring) on the red/green pair of the old phone line. At your wall jack:

1. Identify which two wires go out to the gate controller (usually red + green, sometimes yellow + black on a second line).
2. Disconnect them from the dead telco side of the jack.
3. Run them into the **FXS / Phone / Line 1** port of the ATA or cellular terminal (just an RJ11 cable — cut one end, wire the middle two conductors).
4. Program your mobile number into the gate controller as the "call" number for your unit (done via the keypad at the gate or its programming interface — check the manual for your specific unit).

When a visitor punches your code, the gate dials your cell, you press 9 (or whatever your system uses) to open it.

## Things to watch for
- **Ring voltage and loop current**: cheap ATAs sometimes don't provide enough to trigger very old gate boards. Grandstream and Cisco are generally fine. If yours doesn't trigger, a "ring booster" module fixes it.
- **DTMF passthrough**: make sure the device passes touch-tones reliably (set to RFC2833 on VoIP), or the "press 9 to open" won't work.
- **DTMF from your cell**: some carriers (especially on VoLTE) mangle touch tones. Test before committing.

## HOA note
Since the gate controller is typically inside your unit (or at least the wiring terminates there), you're just changing what's on your side of the demarc — you're not modifying HOA equipment. But if the controller is in a shared space, get permission first.

Tell me the make/model of the gate entry system and whether the controller lives in your unit or at the gate, and I can get more specific.

Here is how you can bridge your mobile phone or a dedicated SIM to your gate system.

### 1. The Hardware Solution: GSM Gateway
You do not need to "rig" anything with a soldering iron; there are off-the-shelf devices that act as a bridge.

*   **The Device:** Look for a **"GSM Fixed Wireless Terminal" (FWT)**. These are widely available on Amazon or eBay.
*   **How it works:** You insert a SIM card (some carriers offer "data-only" or "talk-only" SIMs for cheap) into the device. The device has an RJ11 port on the back.
*   **The Connection:** You plug a standard phone cord from the RJ11 port on the gateway into your wall jack. 
    *   *Crucial Step:* **You must disconnect your unit from the building’s main telephone network.** If you don't, you will be back-feeding your signal into the building's dead lines, which could damage the equipment or cause a short. You need to find the "demarcation point" inside your unit and ensure your internal wiring is isolated from the building's external wiring.

### 2. The "Bluetooth" Alternative
If you don't want to pay for a second SIM card, you need a **Bluetooth-to-Landline Bridge** (often marketed as a "Cell2Jack").

*   **The Device:** A **Cell2Jack** or similar Bluetooth gateway.
*   **How it works:** You pair your current smartphone to this device via Bluetooth. When someone calls the gate, the gate system "dials" your unit. The Cell2Jack receives the signal and routes the call through your smartphone.
*   **Pros:** No extra SIM card or monthly plan required.
*   **Cons:** Your smartphone must be within Bluetooth range (usually 30 feet) of the device for it to work.

### 3. The Wiring Diagram (Conceptual)
Since you are plugging into a wall jack, you are essentially turning your apartment's internal wiring into a private "loop."

1.  **Isolate:** Locate the phone panel in your unit. Disconnect the wires coming from the "outside" (the building's main line).
2.  **Bridge:** Connect the RJ11 output of your GSM Gateway or Cell2Jack to any wall jack in your unit.
3.  **Power:** Because the gate system is "ancient," it likely relies on the **Ring Voltage** provided by the phone line to trigger the buzzer. 
    *   *Note:* Most modern GSM gateways provide standard ring voltage, but some very old gate systems require a higher voltage to trigger the physical bell. If the gate calls your phone but the "open" command (usually pressing '9') doesn't work, you may need a **Line Voltage Booster**.

### Important Warnings
*   **The "9" Command:** Most gate systems work by sending a DTMF tone (the beep you hear when you press a button) when you press '9' on your phone. Ensure your chosen gateway supports **DTMF pass-through**. Most do, but it is worth checking the manual.
*   **The HOA/Building Wiring:** If you live in a condo, the wiring inside your walls is technically HOA property. If you disconnect the building's line, ensure you do it cleanly at the junction box so you can reverse it if you ever move out.
*   **Power:** These gateways require a wall outlet. Make sure you have a power source near your phone jack.

### Recommendation
If you want the easiest path, buy a **Cell2Jack**. It is plug-and-play, requires no extra phone plan, and effectively turns your mobile phone into the "landline" that the gate system is looking for. Just ensure your phone is kept in a spot where it maintains a solid Bluetooth connection to the device.

This is a classic problem with older multi-tenant buildings. The good news is that you likely have a misunderstanding of how this system works, and the solution might be incredibly cheap and easy—no hacking required. 

Here is a breakdown of how these systems work, why your proposed Bluetooth idea might actually damage the building's system, and how to actually fix this.

### The "Aha!" Moment: How Old Gate Systems Work
You mentioned the system requires a "physical landline hooked up in your unit." 

In 99% of these older systems (often called "No Phone Bill" intercoms, made by companies like Doorking or Linear), **you do not need active phone service from a telecom company.** You do not need a dial tone. 

The gate system itself acts as a mini telephone company for the building. It is hardwired directly to the phone jacks in your apartment. When someone at the gate dials your unit, the gate system sends a ring voltage down the wire to your wall jack. When you pick up, it connects the audio. When you press "9" on the keypad, it hears the tone and opens the gate.

### Step 1: The $10 Test (Do this first)
Before you buy any complex gateways, do this:
1. Go to a thrift store, Walmart, or Amazon and buy a **basic, cheap, corded analog telephone** (the kind that doesn't even need to plug into a power outlet). 
2. Plug it directly into the phone jack in your wall.
3. Have a friend go to the gate and dial your unit.

If the phone rings, pick it up. If you can hear your friend, press "9" (or whatever your building's code is). If the gate opens, your problem is solved. You just leave that cheap phone plugged into the wall specifically for the gate.

### Step 2: Why a Bluetooth Gateway won't work (and is dangerous)
You asked for a device that "fakes a dial tone" (like a Cell2Jack or a MagicJack). **Do not plug one of these into your wall jack.**

These devices are designed to *provide* voltage and a dial tone to a telephone. Your building's gate system is *also* designed to provide voltage to a telephone. If you plug a dial-tone generator into the wall, you are sending voltage backward into the gate system. Best case scenario, it simply won't work. Worst case scenario, you will fry the gate system's control board, and the HOA will hold you financially responsible.

### Step 3: How to actually route it to your Cell Phone
If the $10 corded phone works, but you absolutely refuse to walk over to the wall to answer it and want it to ring your cell phone, you have two options:

#### Option A: The "Smart Intercom" Bridge (Easiest)
There are consumer products designed specifically to bridge old analog intercoms to your smartphone via Wi-Fi. 
*   **Ring Intercom:** Amazon makes a device specifically for this. You wire it into the wall jack (or into the handset of the cheap corded phone you bought). When the gate system rings the line, the Ring Intercom intercepts it, connects to your Wi-Fi, and rings the Ring app on your cell phone. You can then speak to the person and press a button on your screen to open the gate.
*   **Nuki Opener:** Similar to the Ring Intercom, popular in Europe but works in the US. 

#### Option B: The DIY VoIP Gateway (Complex)
If you want to build a true bridge, you need an **FXO Gateway** (Foreign Exchange Office). An FXO port is designed to receive a ring voltage (acting like a telephone). 
1. You buy an ATA (Analog Telephone Adapter) with an **FXO port** (like a Grandstream HT813).
2. You plug the wall jack into the FXO port.
3. You connect the ATA to your internet router.
4. You configure the ATA to connect to a SIP server (like a free PBX setup or a cheap VoIP provider).
5. You set a rule: "When voltage is detected on the FXO port (the gate is ringing), dial my cell phone number."
6. When you answer your cell phone, you are bridged to the gate, and you can press "9" on your cell phone keypad to open it.

*Note: Option B requires a solid understanding of networking and VoIP configuration.*

### Summary
Don't try to inject a dial tone into your wall. Go buy a $10 corded phone, plug it in, and test the gate. It is highly likely that the physical wiring is still intact and the gate system will ring the phone without you needing an account with a phone company.

I’ve broken it into three parts:

1. **What you need (off‑the‑shelf products)**  
2. **How the pieces connect – a simple wiring diagram**  
3. **Step‑by‑step setup & configuration**

---

## 1. Off‑the‑Shelf Solutions that Already Do the Heavy Lifting  

| Device (or DIY kit) | How it works | Why it’s a good fit for a “cell‑to‑landline” trick | Typical price |
|---------------------|--------------|---------------------------------------------------|---------------|

No custom wiring required. | $70‑$120 |
| **Obi202 / Obi206** (Google‑Voice‑ready) | Similar to the HT801 but adds a **Bluetooth‑to‑USB dongle** (or can be controlled via a Raspberry Pi). It presents a regular telephone line to any device that plugs into the RJ11 port. | Works with any Android/iOS app that can dial a POTS number; you can also use the Obi’s web UI to set “dial‑out” rules that automatically call the gate when you press a button on your phone. | $45‑$80 |
| **Cell‑to‑POTS “gateway” modules** (e.g., **Cox Cell‑to‑POTS**, **VTech CS610**, **Grandstream GXP1620**) | These are small boxes that sit between a cellular SIM and a telephone jack. They generate a dial tone on the jack when they receive a call on the SIM. | You can pair the module with your mobile via Bluetooth (or simply dial the module’s SIM‑number from any phone). The module then “answers” on the landline and holds the line for the gate controller. | $100‑$180 |
| **DIY Raspberry Pi + “RPI‑Phone” board** | A hobbyist board that emulates a telephone line (tip/ring) and can be controlled over Bluetooth or Wi‑Fi. You run Asterisk or a tiny Python script that generates a dial‑tone and sends DTMF when you call a specific number. | Gives you full control – you can make the Pi answer any incoming call, play a pre‑recorded “gate‑open” tone, and even log who opened the gate. | $30‑$60 for parts (Pi, USB sound card, RPI‑Phone board) |

> **Bottom line:** If you want a ready‑made, plug‑and‑play solution, the **Grandstream HT812** (or the similar **Obi202** with a Bluetooth dongle) is the simplest. If you like tinkering, the Raspberry Pi route gives you a customizable “fake‑dial‑tone” that you can trigger from any Bluetooth‑enabled phone.

---

## 2. Wiring / Connection Diagram  

Below is a **generic schematic** that works for any of the devices above. I’ll use the Grandstream HT801/HT812 as the example because it’s the most common “FXS‑to‑VoIP” box that already has a built‑in RJ11 port.

```
   +-------------------+          +-------------------+          +-------------------+
   |   Mobile Phone    |  BT     |  Bluetooth      |  RJ11    |  Wall‑Jack (POTS) |
   |   (any OS)        |<------>|  Adapter /      |--------->|  (Tip / Ring)     |
   |   (dial the gate) |          |  FXS Gateway    |          |                   |
   +-------------------+          +-------------------+          +-------------------+

   (Power)                (Power)                (Power)
   +5 V USB               +5 V USB               48 V DC (idle) from telco
```

### How the connections actually look on the hardware

| Pin / Port | What it is | What you plug into it |
|------------|------------|-----------------------|
| **RJ11 “Line” jack** on the gateway | The *simulated* telephone line that the gate controller sees. | Plug the existing **wall‑jack** (the one that currently feeds the gate) into this port. The gateway will present a *dial tone* on the line. |
| **RJ11 “Phone” jack** (optional) | If the gateway has a second RJ11 for a *second* line, you can use it for a separate device (e.g., a regular phone). | Not needed for the gate, but you can keep it free. |
| **USB / Power input** | Provides the 5 V needed for the gateway’s electronics. | Plug into any wall‑wart or PoE injector (if the model supports PoE). |
| **Bluetooth / Wi‑Fi** | Used to pair the gateway with your phone or to expose a web UI. | Pair your phone (or connect via the gateway’s web interface). |
| **SIP / Web UI** | Configuration interface (usually a browser at `http://192.168.1.XXX`). | Set the “dial‑out” number that the gate expects (often a short 4‑digit code). |

> **Important safety note:** The telephone line from the telco can carry up to **90 V AC ringing** and **48 V DC** when on‑hook. The gateway is designed to handle that automatically, so you **don’t need to add any extra protection** – just plug the RJ11 cable into the wall jack and let the device do the rest.

---

## 3. Step‑by‑Step Setup  

### A. Acquire the hardware  1. **Pick a gateway** – I recommend the **Grandstream HT812** because it has native Bluetooth support (or the HT801 + a cheap Bluetooth‑to‑USB dongle).  
2. **Buy a short RJ11 patch cable** (male‑to‑male) if you don’t already have one.  
3. **Gather a power adapter** (5 V / 1 A USB wall wart) and a power outlet near the gate’s junction box.

### B. Physical installation  
1. **Locate the existing wall jack** that feeds the gate controller.  
2. **Disconnect the existing telephone line** (if any) and plug the **gateway’s RJ11 “Line” jack** into that wall jack.  3. **Connect the gateway’s power** (USB) to a nearby outlet.  
4. **Pair your mobile phone** with the gateway via Bluetooth (usually a “BT‑Pair” button on the device; the phone will see a device named something like “HT812‑BT”).  

### C. Configure the gateway  
1. **Open a web browser** on a PC or phone and go to the gateway’s default IP (often `192.168.0.1` or `192.168.1.1`).  
2. **Log in** (default admin / admin).  
3. **Set up the “FXS” line:**  
   - **Line Settings → Line 1** → Enable.  
   - **Dial Tone** – leave as “Default”.  
   - **Call Waiting** – disable (not needed).  
4. **Create a “Speed‑Dial” or “Call‑Out” rule** that matches the gate’s “call‑in” number.  
   - Example: If the gate expects you to dial **`1234`** (a 4‑digit code), set **Speed‑Dial 1** → **Number:** `1234`.  
   - Assign this speed‑dial to a **Bluetooth‑triggered button** (some gateways let you map a Bluetooth “press” to a speed‑dial).  
5. **Save and reboot** the gateway.

### D. Test the connection  1. **From your phone**, open the Bluetooth “Phone” app (or simply use the native dialer).  
2. **Dial the gate’s “call‑in” number** (the same 4‑digit code you entered above).  
3. The gateway should **answer with a dial tone**, hold the line, and then **send the appropriate DTMF** (or just keep the line open).  
4. The gate controller, seeing a normal POTS call, will unlock the gate (or trigger whatever action it’s wired to).  

> **If the gate only reacts to a *ring* and not a dial tone**, you can force the gateway to generate a ring by enabling “Ring Equivalent” in the line settings. Most FXS devices have a “Ring Cadence” option you can set to “1‑second on / 2‑seconds off”.

### E. Optional – Add a “one‑touch” button on your phone  
If you want a single tap instead of dialing a number:  

1. **Create a shortcut** on your phone’s home screen that launches the dialer with the pre‑filled number (e.g., `*1234#`).  
2. **Assign a Bluetooth “media‑button”** (many phones let you map a Bluetooth headset button to “play/pause”).  
3. **Press the headset button** → the dialer opens → the number is sent automatically → gate opens.  

---

## 4. Alternative “DIY” Approach (Raspberry Pi + RPI‑Phone Board)

If you enjoy tinkering, here’s a quick outline:

| Component | Approx. Cost | Role |
|-----------|--------------|------|
| Raspberry Pi Zero W | $10 | Small Linux computer, Bluetooth & Wi‑Fi |
| USB Audio Adapter (e.g., **CM108**) | $5 | Provides the analog audio signals needed for a telephone line |
| **RPI‑Phone** board (or a simple ** optocoupler + relay** circuit) | $15‑$20 | Generates the 48 V DC and ringing signals that a POTS line expects |
| **Micro‑SD card** (8 GB) | $5 | OS & software |
| **Power supply** (5 V / 2 A) | $5 | Powers the Pi |

**Software flow (high‑level):**

1. Install **Asterisk** (or **FreePBX**) on the Pi.  
2. Configure a **“Local” extension** that, when called, runs a script to **activate a relay** that closes the gate’s “open” contact.  
3. Use **BlueZ** (the Linux Bluetooth stack) to pair the Pi with your phone.  
4. When you press “Call” on your phone, the Pi receives the call, answers, and **sends a DTMF “1234”** to the gate’s line.  5. The script also **logs the event** (who opened the gate and when).

**Pros:** Full control, can add logging, can be expanded to support multiple gates.  
**Cons:** Requires soldering, a bit of Linux knowledge, and a small enclosure to protect the electronics from the garage environment.

---

## 5. Things to Keep in Mind  

| Issue | What to watch for |
|-------|-------------------|
| **HOA / Building Rules** | Some communities forbid “modifying” the exterior wiring. Keep the work **inside your unit** (i.e., only plug the gateway into the existing jack) and **don’t cut or splice** the telco line. |
| **Power** | The gateway needs a reliable 5 V source. If the nearest outlet is far, consider a **PoE injector** (many HT812 units support PoE). |
| **Signal Quality** | If the gate is far from your unit, the analog telephone line may suffer from attenuation. A **line‑amplifier** (simple 600 Ω transformer) can be added before the gateway, but most modern FXS boxes handle up to 300 ft without issue. |
| **Security** | The gateway will expose a small web UI. Change the default admin password and, if possible, restrict access to your home LAN only. |
| **Backup** | Keep a **regular phone** (or a cheap cordless handset) plugged into the gateway’s second RJ11 jack. That way, if the Bluetooth link fails, you still have a manual way to open the gate. |

---

| Item | Example Model | Where to buy |

> **Plug a Bluetooth‑enabled FXS gateway (e.g., Grandstream HT812) into the existing wall jack, pair it with your phone, and configure it to answer a call on that line and send the gate’s dial‑in code – no rewiring, no HOA approvals, just a simple “cell‑to‑landline” bridge.**

```text
[Internet router]
      |
      v

      v
```

### BIG WARNING

- a live phone-company line

- any unknown wiring

- **LTE home phone gateway**
- **cellular terminal analog phone port**

These take a **SIM card** and provide:
- dial tone

- a standard analog phone jack


## Analog line 1 uses the center pair
Traditional old phone wiring:
- **Red = Ring**
- **Green = Tip**

Cat3/Cat5 style:
- **White/Blue = Tip**

Usually polarity doesn’t matter for modern phones, but using the normal pair is best.

```text
            v

```

Again: **only after disconnecting any outside source**.

### If:

This is a frustratingly common situation in older condos and gated communities. Before you attempt to wire anything, it is critical to understand how your specific gate system communicates with your unit, because installing the wrong device can damage the gate controller or your equipment.

Here is a breakdown of the technical hurdles, the risks, and the viable solutions.

### 1. Identify the System Type
There are two main types of gate intercom systems. The solution depends entirely on which one you have.

*   **Type A: PSTN Dialer (Most Likely)**
    *   **How it works:** When a visitor presses your button, the gate box acts like a telephone. It seizes the phone line and **dials your specific phone number**.
    *   **The Problem:** If the phone company has disconnected the line at the street, the gate is dialing a dead number.
    *   **Why a "Dial Tone" in your unit won't work:** Putting a device in your unit that generates a dial tone does not help because the gate isn't listening for a tone; it's trying to place a call. Unless the HOA reprograms the gate to dial your *cell phone number* (or the number of a cellular gateway), the signal never reaches your unit.
*   **Type B: Hardwired Intercom (Legacy)**
    *   **How it works:** The gate box is directly wired to your unit via a dedicated pair of copper wires. Pressing the button sends a low-voltage DC signal or ring voltage directly down that wire to ring a bell or handset in your unit.
    *   **The Problem:** If the phone company cut the copper pair outside the building, the circuit is broken.
    *   **The Fix:** You would need a device that detects the voltage signal on that wire and triggers your cell phone.

### 2. The Risk of "Rigging" a Gateway
You mentioned using a Bluetooth or Cellular gateway to "trick the wall jack." **Proceed with extreme caution.**

*   **Voltage Conflict:** If your gate system is a Dialer (Type A), it outputs voltage to seize the line. If you plug in a Cellular Gateway (which also outputs voltage to simulate a phone line), you are connecting two power sources together. This can fry the gate controller board or the gateway.
*   **Interference:** In multi-unit buildings, the phone wiring is often daisy-chained. Connecting an active device to your jack can send signals back down the line to other units or the main gate box, causing constant ringing or system lockups for your neighbors.
*   **HOA Liability:** Modifying the interface to a common area security system often violates HOA covenants. If your device causes the gate to fail for the whole community, you could be held liable for repair costs.

### 3. Viable Solutions

#### Option A: The Cellular Gateway (Requires HOA Cooperation)
If the system is a **PSTN Dialer**, the only way to make this work without a landline is to change the destination number.
1.  **Purchase a GSM Fixed Wireless Terminal (FWT):** These are devices (often called "Cellular Home Phone Adapters") that take a SIM card and provide a standard phone jack.
2.  **The Catch:** You cannot just plug this into your wall. You must give the SIM card's phone number to the HOA/Property Manager.
3.  **The Fix:** They must program the gate system to dial **that specific cell number** when your button is pressed.
4.  **Result:** The gate calls the SIM, the FWT rings, and you answer. (Note: Many FWTs do not support remote door release tones, so you might be able to talk but not buzz them in unless the FWT supports DTMF pass-through).

#### Option B: Independent Wireless Intercom (No HOA Permission Needed)
If the HOA refuses to touch the gate programming, you must bypass their system entirely.
1.  **Install a Video Doorbell at the Gate (If possible):** Some communities allow residents to install their own cellular call boxes next to the main gate. Devices like **GateSmart** or **ButterflyMX** have cellular options. *Check HOA rules first.*
2.  **Wireless Intercom Bridge:** You can hire a low-voltage security technician to install a **wireless bridge**.
    *   A transmitter is installed at the gate (powered by the gate box).
    *   A receiver is installed in your unit.
    *   When the gate button is pressed, it triggers the wireless signal to your unit, which can then trigger a cellular call or a local chime.
    *   *Note:* This requires running a wire from the gate button to the transmitter, which usually requires HOA approval.

#### Option C: The "Line Simulator" (For Hardwired Systems Only)
If you confirm you have a **Hardwired Intercom (Type B)** and the wiring inside the building is intact (only the service entry is cut):
*   You need a **Telephone Line Simulator** (often used for alarm systems).
*   **Warning:** This does not allow you to answer on your cell. It simply tricks the gate into thinking the line is active so it doesn't throw an error. You would still need a physical handset plugged into that simulator to answer the door. This does not solve your goal of using your mobile phone.

### 4. Recommended Next Steps

When you press the button on your wall panel, it creates a physical short circuit across two specific wires, which sends a relay signal back to the gate to open. 

If you plug a Bluetooth gateway (like an XLink) or an ATA (like an Obihai) into that wall jack, the gateway will look for a dial tone, find nothing, and do nothing. Worse, sending voltage from a gateway *into* the intercom wire could fry the gate's circuit board.

Here are the two actual ways to solve this.

---

### Solution 1: The "Off-the-Shelf" Hack (Ring Intercom)
You don't actually have to build this from scratch. A company called Ring makes a device specifically designed to exploit exactly the type of wiring you have.

*   **The Product:** [Ring Intercom](https://shop.ring.com/products/intercom)
*   **How it works:** It replaces your wall panel. You take your current wall plate off, disconnect the two to four wires attached to it, and connect those wires to the Ring Intercom module. 
*   **The Magic:** The Ring module is able to steal the tiny bit of DC power traveling over those wires to power its own Wi-Fi chip. It connects to your home Wi-Fi, and whenever someone buzzes the gate, it sends a notification to your phone via the Ring app. You can talk to them and press a button on your screen to trigger the gate relay.
*   **Caveat:** It requires Wi-Fi signal near your front door. If your router is far away, you may need a cheap Wi-Fi extender plugged into a nearby outlet.

---

### Solution 2: The True DIY "Rig" (Shelly Relay)
If you don't want to use Ring, or if your specific intercom system is too obscure for Ring to trigger the relay, you can build a Wi-Fi relay switch for about $25. 

*Note: This solution will let you buzz people in from your phone, but it may not allow you to speak to them through your phone (audio is very difficult to hack). For 90% of people (UberEats, Amazon, friends), just being able to remotely hit the "unlock" button is all they care about.*

**What you need:**
1.  **Shelly Plus 1** (A tiny Wi-Fi relay switch that fits inside a wall box). ~$20
2.  A phone wire with RJ11 connectors on both ends. ~$5
3.  A small USB power bank (optional, only if the intercom wire doesn't carry enough voltage to power the Shelly).

**The Conceptual Wiring Diagram:**
1.  **Remove the wall plate.** You will see wires connected to terminals usually labeled something like "TIP", "RING", "GND", or "LOCK".
2.  **Identify the button wires.** Take a wire jumper and touch it across the "TIP" and "RING" (or "GND" and "LOCK") terminals. If you hear the gate click open, you found the right two wires.
3.  **Connect the Shelly.** 
    *   Take your phone cord and cut off one end. Strip the outer jacket to reveal the red, green, yellow, and black wires inside. 
    *   Connect the **Green** and **Red** wires to the two terminals you identified in step 2. (These are the standard "Tip" and "Ring" wires in phone cabling).
    *   Connect the other end of the Green and Red wires to the **O (Output)** and **S (Switch)** terminals on the Shelly Plus 1.
4.  **Power the Shelly.** The Shelly needs 12V-24V to run. Touch the Shelly's power inputs to the other wires on the wall plate (usually Yellow and Black). If the Shelly's LED lights up, the intercom system is providing enough power! If it doesn't light up, you will need to plug the Shelly's USB-C power cable into a small USB charger hidden behind the wall plate.
5.  **Setup.** Download the Shelly app, connect the Shelly to your Wi-Fi. 
6.  **Use it.** Whenever you need to open the gate, you open the Shelly app on your phone and tap the power button. It physically closes the circuit, exactly as if you pressed the button on the wall.

### A Final Warning
Because you are dealing with low-voltage wiring that ultimately connects to a very expensive gate motor at the street, **do not use external power sources (like a 12V wall wart) to send power *down* the phone wire to the gate.** Only use external power to power the Shelly locally. Sending the wrong voltage to the gate panel is a fast way to buy your HOA a new gate operator out of your own pocket.
